To bear it tamely; touch me with noble anger,
And let not women's weapons, water-drops,
Stain my man's cheeks! No, you unnatural hags,
I will have such revenges on you both,
That all the world shall--I will do such things--
What they are, yet I know not; but they shall be
The terrors of the earth. You think I'll weep;
No, I'll not weep:
I have full cause of weeping; but this heart
Shall break into a hundred thousand flaws,

Or ere I'll weep. O fool, I shall go mad!
[Exeunt Lear, Gloucester, Kent, and Fool.
Storm and tempest.

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.p: Let us withdraw; 'twill be a storm.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l:
This house is little: the old man and
his people
Cannot be well bestow'd.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l:
'Tis his own blame; hath put himself
from rest,
And must needs taste his folly.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l:
For this particular, I'll receive him
gladly,
But not one follower.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: So am I purposed.
Where is my lord of Gloucester?

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.l:
Follow'd the old man forth: he is
return'd.
Re-enter GLOUCESTER.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: The king is in high rage.

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.l: Whither is he going?

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l:
He calls to horse; but will I know not
whither.

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.l:
'Tis best to give him way; he leads
himself.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l:
My lord, entreat him by no means to
stay.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l:
Alack, the night comes on, and the
bleak winds
Do sorely ruffle; for many miles about
There's scarce a bush.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: O, sir, to wilful men,
The injuries that they themselves procure
Must be their schoolmasters. Shut up your doors:
He is attended with a desperate train;
And what they may incense him to, being apt
To have his ear abused, wisdom bids fear.

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.l:
Shut up your doors, my lord; 'tis a
wild night:
My Regan counsels well: come out o' the storm. [Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE I
div.stage:
Enter KENT and a Gentleman,
meeting.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Who's there, besides foul weather?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p:
One minded like the weather, most
unquietly.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: I know you. Where's the king?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Contending with the fretful element:
Bids the wind blow the earth into the sea,
Or swell the curled waters 'bove the main,

That things might change or cease; tears his
white hair,
Which the impetuous blasts, with eyeless rage,
Catch in their fury, and make nothing of;
Strives in his little world of man to out-scorn
The to-and-fro-conflicting wind and rain.

This night, wherein the cub-drawn bear would
couch,
The lion and the belly-pinched wolf
Keep their fur dry, unbonneted he runs,
And bids what will take all.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l: But who is with him?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l:
None but the fool; who labours to
out-jest
His heart-struck injuries.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l: Sir, I do know you;
And dare, upon the warrant of my note,
Commend a dear thing to you. There is division,
Although as yet the face of it be cover'd

With mutual cunning, 'twixt Albany and
Cornwall;
Who have--as who have not, that their great stars

Throned and set high?--servants, who seem no
less,
Which are to France the spies and speculations
Intelligent to our state; what hath been seen,
Either in snuffs and packings of the dukes,
Or the hard rein which both of them have borne
Against the old kind king; or something deeper,
Whereof perchance these are but furnishings;
But, true it is, from France there comes a power
Into this scatter'd kingdom; who already,
Wise in our negligence, have secret feet
In some of our best ports, and are at point
To show their open banner. Now to you:
If on my credit you dare build so far
To make your speed to Dover, you shall find
Some that will thank you, making just report
Of how unnatural and bemadding sorrow
The king hath cause to plain.
I am a gentleman of blood and breeding;
And, from some knowledge and assurance, offer
This office to you.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: I will talk further with you.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l: No, do not.
For confirmation that I am much more
Than my out-wall, open this purse and take
What it contains. If you shall see Cordelia,--
As fear not but you shall,--show her this ring;
And she will tell you who your fellow is
That yet you do not know. Fie on this storm!
I will go seek the king.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p:
Give me your hand: have you no more
to say?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l:
Few words, but, to effect, more than
all yet;

That, when we have found the king,--in which,
your pain
That way, I'll this,--he that first lights on him
Holla the other. [Exeunt severally.

div.head: SCENE II
div.stage:
Another part of the heath. Storm
still.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l:
Blow, winds, and crack your cheeks!
rage! blow!
You cataracts and hurricanoes, spout

Till you have drench'd our steeples, drown'd the
cocks!
You sulphurous and thought-executing fires,
Vaunt-couriers to oak-cleaving thunderbolts,

Singe my white head! And thou, all-shaking
thunder,
Smite flat the thick rotundity o' the world!
Crack nature's moulds, all germens spill at once,
That make ingrateful man!

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.p: O nuncle, court holy-water in a dry house is better than this rain-water out o' door. Good nuncle, in, and ask thy daughters' blessing: here's a night pities neither wise man nor fool.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l:
Rumble thy bellyful! Spit, fire!
spout, rain!
Nor rain, wind, thunder, fire, are my daughters:
I tax not you, you elements with unkindness;
I never gave you kingdom, call'd you children,
You owe me no subscription: then let fall
Your horrible pleasure; here I stand, your slave,
A poor, infirm, weak, and despised old man:
But yet I call you servile ministers,
That have with two pernicious daughters join'd
Your high engender'd battles 'gainst a head
So old and white as this. O! O! 'tis foul!

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.p: He that has a house to put's head in has a good head-piece. The cod-piece that will house Before the head has any, The head and he shall louse; So beggars marry many. The man that makes his toe What he his heart should make Shall of a corn cry woe, And turn his sleep to wake. For there was never yet fair woman but she made mouths in a glass.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: No, I will be the pattern of all patience;

I will say nothing.
Enter KENT.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Who's there?

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.p: Marry, here's grace and a cod-piece; that's a wise man and a fool.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l:
Alas, sir, are you here? things that
love night
Love not such nights as these; the wrathful skies
Gallow the very wanderers of the dark,
And make them keep their caves: since I was man,
Such sheets of fire, such bursts of horrid thunder,
Such groans of roaring wind and rain, I never

Remember to have heard: man's nature cannot
carry
The affliction nor the fear.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: Let the great gods,
That keep this dreadful pother o'er our heads,

Find out their enemies now. Tremble, thou
wretch,
That hast within thee undivulged crimes,
Unwhipp'd of justice: hide thee, thou bloody hand;
Thou perjured, and thou simular man of virtue
That art incestuous: caitiff, to pieces shake,
That under covert and convenient seeming
Hast practised on man's life: close pent-up guilts,
Rive your concealing continents, and cry
These dreadful summoners grace. I am a man
More sinn'd against than sinning.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l: Alack, bare-headed!
Gracious my lord, hard by here is a hovel;

Some friendship will it lend you 'gainst the
tempest:
Repose thou there; while I to this hard house--
More harder than the stones whereof 'tis raised;
Which even but now, demanding after you,
Denied me to come in--return, and force
Their scanted courtesy.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: My wits begin to turn.
Come on, my boy: how dost, my boy? art cold?
I am cold myself. Where is this straw, my fellow?
The art of our necessities is strange,

That can make vile things precious. Come, your
hovel.
Poor fool and knave, I have one part in my heart
That's sorry yet for thee.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l:
[Singing] He that has and a little tiny
wit,--
With hey, ho, the wind and the rain,--
Must make content with his fortunes fit,
For the rain it raineth every day.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
True, my good boy. Come, bring us
to this hovel. [Exeunt Lear and Kent.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: This is a brave night to cool a courtezan.
I'll speak a prophecy ere I go:
When priests are more in word than matter;
When brewers mar their malt with water;
When nobles are their tailors' tutors;
No heretics burn'd, but wenches' suitors;
When every case in law is right;
No squire in debt, nor no poor knight;
When slanders do not live in tongues;
Nor cutpurses come not to throngs;
When usurers tell their gold i' the field;
And bawds and whores do churches build;
Then shall the realm of Albion
Come to great confusion:
Then comes the time, who lives to see't,
That going shall be used with feet.

This prophecy Merlin shall make; for I live
before his time. [Exit.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: Alack, alack, Edmund, I like not this unnatural dealing. When I desire their leave that I might pity him, they took from me the use of mine own house; charged me, on pain of their perpetual displeasure, neither to speak of him, entreat for him, nor any way sustain him.

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.p: Most savage and unnatural!

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: Go to; say you nothing. There's a division betwixt the dukes: and a worse matter than that: I have received a letter this night; 'tis dangerous to be spoken; I have locked the letter in my closet: these injuries the king now bears will be revenged home; there's part of a power already footed: we must incline to the king. I will seek him, and privily relieve him: go you and maintain talk with the duke, that my charity be not of him perceived: if he ask for me, I am ill, and gone to bed. Though I die for it, as no less is threatened me, the king my old master must be relieved. There is some strange thing toward, Edmund; pray you, be careful. [Exit.

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.l: This courtesy, forbid thee, shall the duke
Instantly know; and of that letter too:
This seems a fair deserving, and must draw me
That which my father loses; no less than all.
The younger rises when the old doth fall. [Exit.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l:
Here is the place, my lord; good my
lord, enter:
The tyranny of the open night's too rough
For nature to endure. [Storm still.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: Let me alone.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l: Good my lord, enter here.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: Wilt break my heart?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l:
I had rather break mine own. Good
my lord, enter.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l:
Thou think'st 'tis much that this
contentious storm
Invades us to the skin: so 'tis to thee;
But where the greater malady is fix'd,
The lesser is scarce felt. Thou'ldst shun a bear;
But if thy flight lay toward the raging sea,

Thou'ldst meet the bear i' the mouth. When
the mind's free,
The body's delicate: the tempest in my mind
Doth from my senses take all feeling else
Save what beats there. Filial ingratitude!
Is it not as this mouth should tear this hand
For lifting food to 't? But I will punish home:
No, I will weep no more. In such a night
To shut me out! Pour on; I will endure.
Tn such a night as this! O Regan, Goneril!
Your old kind father, whose frank heart gave all,--
O, that way madness lies; let me shun that;
No more of that.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l: Good my lord, enter here.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l:
Prithee, go in thyself; seek thine own
ease:
This tempest will not give me leave to ponder
On things would hurt me more. But I'll go in.

[To the Fool] In, boy; go first. You houseless
poverty,--

Nay, get thee in. I'll pray, and then I'll sleep.
[Fool goes in.
Poor naked wretches, wheresoe'er you are,
That bide the pelting of this pitiless storm,
How shall your houseless heads and unfed sides,
Your loop'd and window'd raggedness, defend you
From seasons such as these? O, I have ta'en
Too little care of this! Take physic, pomp;
Expose thyself to feel what wretches feel,
That thou mayst shake the superflux to them,
And show the heavens more just.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p:
Fathom and half, fathom and half! Poor Tom!
[The Fool runs out from the hovel.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Come not in here, nuncle, here's aspirit.
Help me, help me!

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Give me thy hand. Who's there?

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.p: A spirit, a spirit: he says his name's poor Tom.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
What art thou that dost grumble there i' the straw? Come forth.
Enter EDGAR disguised as a madman.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: Away! the foul fiend follows me!
Through the sharp hawthorn blows the cold wind.
Hum! go to thy cold bed, and warm thee.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: Hast thou given all to thy two daughters?
And art thou come to this?

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: Who gives any thing to poor Tom? whom the foul fiend hath led through fire and through flame, through ford and whirli-pool, o'er bog and quagmire; that hath laid knives under his pillow, and halters in his pew; set ratsbane by his porridge; made him proud of heart, to ride on a bay trotting-horse over four-inched bridges, to course his own shadow for a traitor. Bless thy five wits! Tom's a-cold,--O, do de, do de, do de. Bless thee from whirlwinds, star-blasting, and taking! Do poor Tom some charity, whom the foul fiend vexes: there could I have him now, --and there,--and there again, and there. [Storm still.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l:
What, have his daughters brought him
to this pass?

Couldst thou save nothing? Didst thou give them
all?

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.p: Nay, he reserved a blanket, else we had been all shamed.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l:
Now, all the plagues that in the
pendulous air

Hang fated o'er men's faults light on thy
daughters!

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: He hath no daughters, sir.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l:
Death, traitor! nothing could have
subdued nature
To such a lowness but his unkind daughters.
Is it the fashion, that discarded fathers
Should have thus little mercy on their flesh?
Judicious punishment! 'twas this flesh begot
Those pelican daughters.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: Pillicock sat on Pillicock-hill:
Halloo, halloo, loo, loo!

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.p: This cold night will turn us all to fools and madmen.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: Take heed o' the foul fiend: obey thy parents; keep thy word justly; swear not; commit not with man's sworn spouse; set not thy sweet heart on proud array. Tom's a-cold.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: What hast thou been?

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p:
A serving-man, proud in heart and mind; that curled my hair; wore gloves in my cap; served the lust of my mistress' heart, and did the act of darkness with her; swore as many oaths as I spake words, and broke them in the sweet face of heaven: one that slept in the contriving of lust, and waked to do it: wine loved I deeply, dice dearly; and in woman out-paramoured the Turk: false of heart, light of ear, bloody of hand; hog in sloth, fox in stealth, wolf in greediness, dog in madness, lion in prey. Let not the creaking of shoes nor the rustling of silks betray thy poor heart to woman: keep thy foot out of brothels, thy hand out of plackets, thy pen from lenders' books, and defy the foul fiend. Still through the hawthorn blows the cold wind: Says suum, mun, ha, no, nonny. Dolphin my boy, my boy, sessa! let him trot by.
[Storm still.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Why, thou wert better in thy grave than to answer with thy uncovered body this extremity of the skies. Is man no more than this? Consider him well. Thou owest the worm no silk, the beast no hide, the sheep no wool, the cat no perfume. Ha! here's three on 's are sophisticated! Thou art the thing itself: unaccommodated man is no more but such a poor, bare, forked animal as thou art. Off, off, you lendings! come, unbutton here. [Tearing off his clothes.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.p:
Prithee, nuncle, be contented; 'tis a naughty night to swim in. Now a little fire in a wild field were like an old lecher's heart; a small spark, all the rest on's body cold. Look, here comes a walking fire.
Enter GLOUCESTER, with a torch.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: S. Withold footed thrice the old;
He met the night-mare, and her nine-fold;
Bid her alight,
And her troth plight,
And, aroint thee, witch, aroint thee!

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: How fares your grace?

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: What's he?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Who's there? What is't you seek?

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: What are you there? Your names?

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: But mice and rats, and such small deer,
Have been Tom's food for seven long year.

Beware my follower. Peace, Smulkin; peace,
thou fiend!

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p:
What, hath your grace no better
company?

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: The prince of darkness is a gentle-
man: Modo he's call'd, and Mahu.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l:
Our flesh and blood is grown so vile,
my lord,
That it doth hate what gets it.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: Poor Tom's a-cold.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: Go in with me: my duty cannot suffer
To obey in all your daughters' hard commands:
Though their injunction be to bar my doors,
And let this tyrannous night take hold upon you,
Yet have I ventured to come seek you out,
And bring you where both fire and food is ready.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: First let me talk with this philosopher.
What is the cause of thunder?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l:
Good my lord, take his offer; go into
the house.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l:
I'll talk a word with this same learned
Theban.
What is your study?

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p:
How to prevent the fiend, and to kill
vermin.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Let me ask you one word in private.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l:
Importune him once more to go, my
lord;
His wits begin to unsettle.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: Canst thou blame him? [Storm still.
His daughters seek his death; ah, that good Kent!
He said it would be thus, poor banish'd man!

Thou say'st the king grows mad; I'll tell thee,
friend.
I am almost mad myself: I had a son,
Now outlaw'd from my blood: he sought my life,
But lately, very late: I loved him, friend:
No father his son dearer: truth to tell thee,

The grief hath crazed my wits. What a night's
this!
I do beseech your grace,--

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: O, cry you mercy, sir.
Noble philosopher, your company.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: Tom's a-cold.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l:
In, fellow, there, into the hovel: keep
thee warm.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: Come, let's in all.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l: This way, my lord.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: With him;
I will keep still with my philosopher.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
Good my lord, soothe him; let him
take the fellow.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: Take him you on.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Sirrah, come on; go along with us.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Come, good Athenian.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: No words, no words: hush.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: Child Rowland to the dark tower came,
His word was still,--Fie, foh, and fum,

I smell the blood of a British man.
[Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.p: I will have my revenge ere I depart his house.

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.p: How, my lord, I may be censured, that nature thus gives way to loyalty, something fears me to think of.

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.p: I now perceive, it was not altogether your brother's evil disposition made him seek his death; but a provoking merit set a-work by a reproveable badness in himself.

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.p: How malicious is my fortune that I must repent to be just! This is the letter he spoke of, which approves him an intelligent party to the advantages of France. O heavens! that this treason were not, or not I the detector!

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.p: Go with me to the duchess.

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.p: If the matter of this paper be certain, you have mighty business in hand.

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.p: True or false, it hath made thee earl of Gloucester. Seek out where thy father is, that be may he ready for our apprehension.

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.p: If I find him comforting the king. it will stuff his suspicion more fully.--I will persevere in my course of loyalty, though the conflict be sore between that and my blood.

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.p: I will lay trust upon thee; and thou shalt find a dearer father in my love. [Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE VI
div.stage:
A chamber in a farmhouse
adjoining the castle.

Enter GLOUCESTER, LEAR, KENT, Fool, and
EDGAR.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: Here is better than the open air; take it thankfully. I will piece out the comfort with what addition I can: I will not be long from you.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: All the power of his wits have given way to his impatience: the gods reward your kindness! [Exit Gloucester.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: Frateretto calls me; and tells me
Nero is an angler in the lake of darkness.
Pray, innocent, and beware the foul fiend.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.p: Prithee, nuncle, tell me whether a madman be a gentleman or a yeoman?

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: A king, a king!

sp.speaker: Fool.
Lear.
sp.l:
To have a thousand with red burning
spits
Come hissing in upon 'em,--

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: The foul fiend bites my back.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.p: He's mad that trusts in the tameness of a wolf, a horse's health, a boy's love, or a whore's oath.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l:
It shall be done; I will arraign them
straight.

[To Edgar] Come, sit thou here, most learned
justicer;

[To the Fool] Thou, sapient sir, sit here. Now,
you she foxes!

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: Look, where he stands and glares!
Wantest thou eyes at trial, madam?
Come o'er the bourn, Bessy, to me,--

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Her boat hath a leak,
And she must not speak
Why she dares not come over to thee.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: The foul fiend haunts poor Tom in the voice of a nightingale. Hopdance cries in Tom's belly for two white herring. Croak not, black angel; I have no food for thee.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l:
How do you, sir? Stand you not so
amazed:
Will you lie down and rest upon the cushions?

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l:
I'll see their trial first. Bring in the
evidence.

[To Edgar] Thou robed man of justice, take thy
place;
[To the Fool] And thou, his yoke-fellow of equity,

Bench by his side: [To Kent] you are o' the
commission,
Sit you too.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: Let us deal justly.
Sleepest or wakest thou, jolly shepherd?
Thy sheep be in the corn;
And for, one blast of thy minikin mouth,
Thy sheep shall take no harm.
Pur! the cat is gray.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Arraign her first: 'tis Goneril. I here take my oath before this honourable assembly, she kicked the poor king her father.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.p: Come hither, mistress. Is your name Goneril?

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: She cannot deny it.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.p: Cry you mercy, I took you for a joint-stool.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l:
And here's another, whose warp'd looks
proclaim
What store her heart is made on. Stop her there!
Arms, arms, sword, fire! Corruption in the place!
False justicer, why hast thou let her 'scape?

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: Bless thy five wits!

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l: O pity! Sir, where is the patience now,
That you so oft have boasted to retain?

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l:
[Aside] My tears begin to take his part
so much,
They'll mar my counterfeiting.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: The little dogs and all,

Tray, Blanch, and Sweet-heart, see, they bark
at me.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: Tom will throw his head at them. Avaunt, you curs!
sp.l: Be thy mouth or black or white,
Tooth that poisons if it bite;
Mastiff, greyhound, mongrel grim,
Hound or spaniel, brach or lym,
Or bobtail tyke or trundle-tail,
Tom will make them weep and wail:
For, with throwing thus my head.
Dogs leap the hatch, and all are fled.
Do de, de, de. Sessa! Come, march to wakes
and fairs and market-towns. Poor Tom, thy horn is dry.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Then let them anatomize Regan; see what breeds about her heart. Is there any cause in nature that makes these hard hearts? [To Edgar] You, sir, I entertain for one of my hundred; only I do not like the fashion of your garments: you will say they are Persian attire; but let them be changed.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Now, good my lord, lie here and rest awhile.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Make no noise, make no noise; draw the curtains: so, so, so. We'll go to supper i' the morning. So, so, so.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l:
And I'll go to bed at noon.
Re-enter GLOUCESTER.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l:
Come hither, friend: where is the king
my master?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l:
Here, sir; but trouble him not, his wits
are gone.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l:
Good friend, I prithee, take him in thy
arms;
I have o'erheard a plot of death upon him:
There is a litter ready; lay him in 't,

And drive towards Dover, friend, where thou
shalt meet

Both welcome and protection. Take up thy
master:
If thou shouldst dally half an hour, his life,
With thine, and all that offer to defend him,
Stand in assured loss: take up, take up;
And follow me, that will to some provision
Give thee quick conduct.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l: Oppressed nature sleeps:

This rest might yet have balm'd thy broken
senses,
Which, if convenience will not allow,

Stand in hard cure. [To the Fool] Come, help
to bear thy master;
Thou must not stay behind.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l:
Come, come, away.
[Exeunt all but Edgar.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l:
When we our betters see bearing our
woes,
We scarcely think our miseries our foes.
Who alone suffers suffers most i' the mind,
Leaving free things and happy shows behind:
But then the mind much sufferance doth o'er-skip,
When grief hath mates, and bearing fellowship.
How light and portable my pain seems now,

When that which makes me bend makes the king
bow,
He childed as I father'd! Tom, away!
Mark the high noises; and thyself bewray,

When false opinion, whose wrong thought defiles
thee,
In thy just proof, repeals and reconciles thee.
What will hap more to-night, safe 'scape the king!
Lurk, lurk. [Exit.

div.head: SCENE VII
div.stage:
Enter CORNWALL, REGAN, GONERIL, EDMUND,
and Servants.

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.p:
Post speedily to my lord your husband; show him this letter: the army of France is landed. Seek out the villain Gloucester.
[Exeunt some of the Servants.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p: Hang him instantly.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p: Pluck out his eyes.

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.p:
Leave him to my displeasure. Edmund, keep you our sister company: the revenges we are bound to take upon your traitorous father are not fit for your beholding. Advise the duke, where you are going, to a most festinate preparation: we are bound to the like. Our posts shall be swift and intelligent betwixt us. Farewell, dear sister: farewell, my lord of Gloucester.
Enter OSWALD. How now! where's the king?

sp.speaker: Osw.
sp.l:
My lord of Gloucester hath convey'd
him hence:
Some five or six and thirty of his knights,
Hot questrists after him, met him at gate;
Who, with some other of the lords dependants,

Are gone with him towards Dover; where they
boast
To have well-armed friends.

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.l: Get horses for your mistress.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: Farewell, sweet lord, and sister.

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.l:
Edmund, farewell.
[Exeunt Goneril, Edmund, and Oswald.
Go seek the traitor Gloucester,

Pinion him like a thief, bring him before us.
[Exeunt other Servants.
Though well we may not pass upon his life
Without the form of justice, yet our power
Shall do a courtesy to our wrath, which men

May blame, but not control. Who's there? the
traitor?
Enter GLOUCESTER, brought in by two or three.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p: Ingrateful fox! 'tis he.

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.p: Bind fast his corky arms.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l:
What mean your graces? Good my
friends, consider
You are my guests: do me no foul play, friends.

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.l: Bind him, I say. [Servants bind him.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: Hard, hard. O filthy traitor!

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: Unmerciful lady as you are, I'm none.

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.l:
To this chair bind him. Villain, thou
shalt find-- [Regan plucks his beard.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: By the kind gods, 'tis most ignobly done
To pluck me by the beard.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: So white, and such a traitor!

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: Naughty lady,

These hairs, which thou dost ravish from my
chin,
Will quicken, and accuse thee: I am your host:
With robbers' hands my hospitable favours
You should not ruffle thus. What will you do?

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.p:
Come, sir, what letters had you late
from France?

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p:
Be simple answerer, for we know the
truth.

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.l:
And what confederacy have you with
the traitors
Late footed in the kingdom?

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l:
To whose hands have you sent the
lunatic king?
Speak.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: I have a letter guessingly set down,
Which came from one that's of a neutral heart,
And not from one opposed.

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.l: Cunning.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: And false.

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.l: Where hast thou sent the king?

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: To Dover.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l:
Wherefore to Dover? Wast thou not
charged at peril--

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.l:
Wherefore to Dover? Let him first
answer that.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l:
I am tied to the stake, and I must stand
the course.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: Wherefore to Dover, sir?

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: Because I would not see thy cruel nails
Pluck out his poor old eyes; nor thy fierce sister
In his anointed flesh stick boarish fangs.
The sea, with such a storm as his bare head
In hell-black night endured, would have buoy'd up,
And quench'd the stelled fires:
Yet, poor old heart, he holp the heavens to rain.
If wolves had at thy gate howl'd that stern time,

Thou shouldst have said 'Good porter, turn the
key,'
All cruels else subscribed: but I shall see
The winged vengeance overtake such children.

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.l:
See't shalt thou never. Fellows, hold
the chair.
Upon these eyes of thine I'll set my foot.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: He that will think to live till he be old,
Give me some help! O cruel! O you gods!

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p:
One side will mock another; the other
too.

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.l: If you see vengeance,--

sp.speaker: First Serv.
sp.l: Hold your hand, my lord:
I have served you ever since I was a child;
But better service have I never done you
Than now to bid you hold.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: How now, you dog!

sp.speaker: First Serv.
sp.l:
If you did wear a beard upon
your chin,

I'd shake it on this quarrel. What do you
mean?

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.l: My villain! [They draw and fight.

sp.speaker: First Serv.
sp.l:
Nay, then, come on, and take the
chance of anger.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l:
Give me thy sword. A peasant stand
up thus!
[Takes a sword, and runs at him behind.

sp.speaker: First Serv.
sp.l:
O, I am slain! My lord, you
have one eye left
To see some mischief on him. O! [Dies.

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.l:
Lest it see more, prevent it. Out, vile
jelly!
Where is thy lustre now?

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l:
All dark and comfortless. Where's my
son Edmund?
Edmund, enkindle all the sparks of nature,
To quit this horrid act.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: Out, treacherous villain!
Thou call'st on him that hates thee: it was he
That made the overture of thy treasons to us;
Who is too good to pity thee.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: O my follies! then Edgar was abused.
Kind gods, forgive me that, and prosper him!

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l:
Go thrust him out at gates, and let him
smell

His way to Dover. [Exit one with Gloucester.
How is't, my lord? how look you?

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.l: I have received a hurt: follow me, lady.
Turn out that eyeless villain; throw this slave
Upon the dunghill. Regan, I bleed apace:

Untimely comes this hurt: give me your arm.
[Exit Cornwall, led by Regan.

sp.speaker: Second Serv.
sp.l:
I'll never care what wickedness
I do,
If this man come to good.

sp.speaker: Third Serv.
sp.l: If she live long,
And in the end meet the old course of death,
Women will all turn monsters.

sp.speaker: Second Serv.
sp.l:
Let's follow the old earl, and get
the Bedlam
To lead him where he would: his roguish madness
Allows itself to any thing.

sp.speaker: Third Serv.
sp.l:
Go thou: I'll fetch some flax
and white of eggs

To apply to his bleeding face. Now, heaven help
him! [Exeunt severally.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l:
Yet better thus, and known to be
contemn'd,
Than still contemn'd and flatter'd. To be worst,
The lowest and most dejected thing of fortune,
Stands still in esperance, lives not in fear:
The lamentable change is from the best;
The worst returns to laughter. Welcome, then,
Thou unsubstantial air that I embrace!
The wretch that thou hast blown unto the worst

Owes nothing to thy blasts. But who comes here?
Enter GLOUCESTER, led by Old Man.
My father, poorly led? World, world, O world!
But that thy strange mutations make us hate thee,
Life would not yield to age.

sp.speaker: Old Man.
sp.p: O, my good lord, I have been your tenant, and your father's tenant, these fourscore years.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l:
Away, get thee away; good friend, be
gone:
Thy comforts can do me no good at all;
Thee they may hurt.

sp.speaker: Old Man.
sp.l: Alack, sir, you cannot see your way.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l:
I have no way, and therefore want no
eyes;
I stumbled when I saw: full oft 'tis seen,
Our means secure us, and our mere defects
Prove our commodities. O dear son Edgar,
The food of thy abused father's wrath!
Might I but live to see thee in my touch,
I'ld say I had eyes again!

sp.speaker: Old Man.
sp.l: How now! Who's there?

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l:
[Aside]O gods! Who is't can say 'I
am at the worst;?
I am worse than e'er I was.

sp.speaker: Old Man.
sp.l: 'Tis poor mad Tom.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l:
[Aside]And worse I may be yet: the
worst is not
So long as we can say 'This is the worst.'

sp.speaker: Old Man.
sp.l: Fellow, where goest?

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: Is it a beggar-man?

sp.speaker: Old Man.
sp.l: Madman and beggar too.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l:
He has some reason, else he could not
beg.
I' the last night's storm I such a fellow saw;
Which made me think a man a worm: my son
Came then into my mind; and yet my mind

Was then scarce friends with him: I have heard
more since.
As flies to wanton boys, are we to the gods,
They kill us for their sport.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: [Aside]How should this be?
Bad is the trade that must play fool to sorrow,
Angering itself and others.--Bless thee, master!

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: Is that the naked fellow?

sp.speaker: Old Man.
sp.l: Ay, my lord.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l:
Then, prithee, get thee gone: if, for
my sake,
Thou wilt o'ertake us, hence a mile or twain,
I' the way toward Dover, do it for ancient love;
And bring some covering for this naked soul,
Who I'll entreat to lead me.

sp.speaker: Old Man.
sp.l: Alack, sir, he is mad.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l:
'Tis the times' plague, when mad-men
lead the blind.
Do as I bid thee, or rather do thy pleasure;
Above the rest, be gone.

sp.speaker: Old Man.
sp.l:
I'll bring him the best 'parel that
I have,
Come on't what will. [Exit.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: Sirrah, naked fellow,--

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p:
Poor Tom's a-cold. [Aside] I cannot
daub it further.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: Come hither, fellow.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p:
And yet I must.--Bless thy sweet
eyes, they bleed.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: Know'st thou the way to Dover?

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: Both stile and gate, horse-way and foot-path. Poor Tom hath been scared out of his good wits: bless thee, good man's son, from the foul fiend! five fiends have been in poor Tom at once; of lust, as Obidicut; Hobbididance, prince of dumbness; Mahu, of stealing; Modo, of murder; Flibbertigibbet, of moping and mowing, who since possesses chambermaids and waiting-women. So, bless thee, master!

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l:
Here, take this purse, thou whom the
heavens' plagues
Have humbled to all strokes: that I am wretched
Makes thee the happier: heavens, deal so still!
Let the superfluous and lust-dieted man,
That slaves your ordinance, that will not see
Because he doth not feel, feel your power quickly;
So distribution should undo excess,
And each man have enough. Dost thou know Dover?

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: Ay, master.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l:
There is a cliff, whose high and bending
head
Looks fearfully in the confined deep:
Bring me but to the very brim of it,
And I'll repair the misery thou dost bear
With something rich about me: from that place
I shall no leading need.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: Give me thy arm:
Poor Tom shall lead thee. [Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE II
div.stage: Before the Duke of Albany's palace.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l:
Welcome, my lord: I marvel our mild
husband

Not met us on the way.
Enter OSWALD.
Now, where's your master?

sp.speaker: Osw.
sp.l:
Madam, within; but never man so
changed.
I told him of the army that was landed;
He smiled at it: I told him you were coming;

His answer was 'The worse:' of Gloucester's
treachery,
And of the loyal service of his son,
When I inform'd him, then he call'd me sot,
And told me I had turn'd the wrong side out:

What most he should dislike seems pleasant to
him;
What like, offensive.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: Then shall you go no further.
It is the cowish terror of his spirit,
That dares not undertake: he'll not feel wrongs

Which tie him to an answer. Our wishes on
the way

May prove effects. Back, Edmund, to my
brother;
Hasten his musters and conduct his powers:
I must change arms at home, and give the distaff
Into my husband's hands. This trusty servant

Shall pass between us: ere long you are like
to hear,
If you dare venture in your own behalf,

A mistress's command. Wear this; spare speech;
[Giving a favour.
Decline your head: this kiss, if it durst speak,
Would stretch thy spirits up into the air:
Conceive, and fare thee well.

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.l: Yours in the ranks of death.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l:
My most dear Gloucester!
[Exit Edmund.
O, the difference of man and man!
To thee a woman's services are due:
My fool usurps my body.

sp.speaker: Osw.
sp.l:
Madam, here comes my lord.
[Exit.
Enter ALBANY.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: I have been worth the whistle.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: O Goneril!

You are not worth the dust which the rude
wind
Blows in your face. I fear your disposition:
That nature, which contemns it origin,
Cannot be border'd certain in itself;
She that herself will sliver and disbranch
From her material sap, perforce must wither
And come to deadly use.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p: No more; the text is foolish.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l:
Wisdom and goodness to the vile seem
vile:

Filths savour but themselves. What have you
done?
Tigers, not daughters, what have you perform'd?
A father, and a gracious aged man,

Whose reverence even the head-lugg'd bear
would lick,

Most barbarous, most degenerate! have you
madded.
Could my good brother suffer you to do it?
A man, a prince, by him so benefited!
If that the heavens do not their visible spirits
Send quickly down to tame these vile offences,
It will come,
Humanity must perforce prey on itself,
Like monsters of the deep.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: Milk-liver'd man!

That bear'st a cheek for blows, a head for
wrongs:
Who hast not in thy brows an eye discerning
Thine honour from thy suffering; that not know'st
Fools do those villains pity who are punish'd

Ere they have done their mischief. Where's thy
drum?
France spreads his banners in our noiseless land,
With plumed helm thy state begins threats;
Whiles thou, a moral fool, sit'st still, and criest
'Alack, why does he so?'

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: See thyself, devil!
Proper deformity seems not in the fiend
So horrid as in woman.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: O vain fool!

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l:
Thou changed and self-cover'd thing,
for shame,
Be-monster not thy feature. Were't my fitness
To let these hands obey my blood,
They are apt enough to dislocate and tear
Thy flesh and bones: howe'er thou art a fiend,
A woman's shape doth shield thee.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l:
Marry, your manhood now--
Enter a Messenger.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: What news?

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.l:
O, my good lord, the Duke of
Cornwall's dead;
Slain by his servant, going to put out
The other eye of Gloucester.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Gloucester's eyes!

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.l:
A servant that he bred, thrill'd with
remorse,
Opposed against the act, bending his sword
To his great master; who, thereat enraged,
Flew on him, and amongst them fell'd him dead;
But not without that harmful stroke, which since
Hath pluck'd him after.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: This shows you are above,
You justicers, that these our nether crimes
So speedily can venge! But, O poor Gloucester
Lost he his other eye?

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.l: Both, both, my lord.
This letter, madam, craves a speedy answer;
'Tis from your sister.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: [Aside]One way I like this well;
But being widow, and my Gloucester with her,
May all the building in my fancy pluck
Upon my hateful life: another way,
The news is not so tart.--I'll read, and answer. [Exit.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l:
Where was his son when they did take
his eyes?

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.l: Come with my lady hither.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: He is not here.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.l:
No, my good lord; I met him back
again.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Knows he the wickedness?

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.l:
Ay, my good lord; 'twas he inform'd
against him;

And quit the house on purpose, that their
punishment
Might have the freer course.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Gloucester, I live
To thank thee for the love thou show'dst the king,
And to revenge thine eyes. Come hither, friend:
Tell me what more thou know'st. [Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Why the King of France is so suddenly gone back know you the reason?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: Something he left imperfect in the state, which since his coming forth is thought of; which imports to the kingdom so much fear and danger, that his personal return was most required and necessary.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Who hath he left behind him general?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: The Marshal of France, Monsieur
La Far.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Did your letters pierce the queen to any demonstration of grief?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l:
Ay, sir; she took them, read them in
my presence;
And now and then an ample tear trill'd down
Her delicate cheek: it seem'd she was a queen
Over her passion; who, most rebel-like,
Sought to be king o'er her.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l: O, then it moved her.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l:
Not to a rage: patience and sorrow
strove

Who should express her goodliest. You have
seen
Sunshine and rain at once: her smiles and tears
Were like a better way: those happy smilets,
That play'd on her ripe lip, seem'd not to know

What guests were in her eyes: which parted
thence,
As pearls from diamonds dropp'd. In brief,
Sorrow would be a rarity most beloved,
If all could so become it.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l: Made she no verbal question?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l:
'Faith, once or twice she heaved the
name of 'father'
Pantingly forth, as if it press'd her heart:
Cried 'Sisters! sisters! Shame of ladies! sisters!

Kent! father! sisters! What, i' the storm? i'
the night?
Let pity not be believed!' There she shook
The holy water from her heavenly eyes,
And clamour moisten'd: then away she started
To deal with grief alone.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l: It is the stars.
The stars above us, govern our conditions;
Else one self mate and mate could not beget

Such different issues. You spoke not with her
since?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l: Was this before the king return'd?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: No, since.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l:
Well, sir, the poor distressed Lear's i'
the town;
Who sometime, in his better tune, remembers
What we are come about, and by no means
Will yield to see his daughter.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Why, good sir?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l:
A sovereign shame so elbows him: his
own unkindness,
That stripp'd her from his benediction, turn'd her
To foreign casualties, gave her dear rights
To his dog-hearted daughters, these things sting
His mind so venomously, that burning shame
Detains him from Cordelia.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Alack, poor gentleman

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l:
Of Albany's and Cornwall's powers you
heard not?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: 'Tis so, they are afoot.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l:
Well, sir, I'll bring you to our master
Lear,
And leave you to attend him: some dear cause
Will in concealment wrap me up awhile;
When I am known aright, you shall not grieve
Lending me this acquaintance. I pray you, go
Along with me. [Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE IV
div.stage:
Enter, with drum and colours, CORDELIA,
Doctor, and Soldiers.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l:
Alack, 'tis he: why, he was met even
now
As mad as the vex'd sea; singing aloud;
Crown'd with rank fumiter and furrow-weeds,
With bur-docks, hemlock, nettles, cuckoo- flowers,
Darnel, and all the idle weeds that grow
In our sustaining corn. A century send forth;
Search every acre in the high-grown field,

And bring him to our eye. [Exit an Officer.]
What can man's wisdom
In the restoring his bereaved sense?
He that helps him take all my outward worth.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: There is means, madam:
Our foster-nurse of nature is repose,
The which he lacks; that to provoke in him,
Are many simples operative, whose power
Will close the eye of anguish.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: All blest secrets,
All you unpublish'd virtues of the earth,
Spring with my tears! be aidant and remediate
In the good man's distress! Seek, seek for him;
Lest his ungovern'd rage dissolve the life

That wants the means to lead it.
Enter a Messenger.

sp.speaker: Mess.
sp.l: News, madam;
The British powers are marching hitherward.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: 'Tis known before; our preparation stands
In expectation of them. O dear father,
It is thy business that I go about;
Therefore great France
My mourning and important tears hath pitied.
No blown ambition doth our arms incite,
But love, dear love and our aged father's right:
Soon may I hear and see him! [Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: But are my brother's powers set forth?

sp.speaker: Osw.
sp.l: Ay, madam.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: Himself in person there?

sp.speaker: Osw.
sp.l: Madam, with much ado:
Your sister is the better soldier.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l:
Lord Edmund spake not with your lord
at home?

sp.speaker: Osw.
sp.p: No, madam.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l:
What might import my sister's letter
to him?

sp.speaker: Osw.
sp.p: I know not, lady.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l:
'Faith, he is posted hence on serious
matter.

It was great ignorance, Gloucester's eyes being
out,
To let him live: where he arrives he moves
All hearts against us: Edmund, I think, is gone,
In pity of his misery, to dispatch
His nighted life; moreover, to descry
The strength o' the enemy.

sp.speaker: Osw.
sp.p:
I must needs after him, madam, with
my letter.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l:
Our troops set forth to-morrow: stay
with us;
The ways are dangerous.

sp.speaker: Osw.
sp.l: I may not, madam:
My lady charged my duty in this business.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l:
Why should she write to Edmund?
Might not you
Transport her purposes by word? Belike,

Something--I know not what: I'll love thee
much,
Let me unseal the letter.

sp.speaker: Osw.
sp.l: Madam, I had rather--

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l:
I know your lady does not love her
husband;
I am sure of that: and at her late being here
She gave strange oeillades and most speaking looks
To noble Edmund. I know you are of her bosom.

sp.speaker: Osw.
sp.p: I, madam?

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: I speak in understanding; you are, I know 't:
Therefore I do advise you, take this note:
My lord is dead; Edmund and I have talk'd;
And more convenient is he for my hand
Than for your lady's: you may gather more.
If you do find him, pray you, give him this;

And when your mistress hears thus much from
you,
I pray, desire her call her wisdom to her.
So, fare you well.
If you do chance to hear of that blind traitor,
Preferment falls on him that cuts him off.

sp.speaker: Osw.
sp.l:
Would I could meet him, madam! I
should show
What party I do follow.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: Fare thee well. [Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE VI
div.stage:
Enter GLOUCESTER, and EDGAR dressed like a
peasant.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l:
When shall we come to the top of that
same hill?

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l:
You do climb up it now: look, how we
labour.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: Methinks the ground is even.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: Horrible steep.
Hark, do you hear the sea?

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: No, truly.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: Why, then, your other senses grow imperfect
By your eyes' anguish.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: So may it be, indeed:
Methinks thy voice is alter'd; and thou speak'st
In better phrase and matter than thou didst.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l:
You're much deceived: in nothing am
I changed
But in my garments.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: Methinks you're better spoken.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l:
Come on, sir; here's the place: stand
still. How fearful
And dizzy 'tis, to cast one's eyes so low!
The crows and choughs that wing the midway air
Show scarce so gross as beetles: half way down
Hangs one that gathers samphire, dreadful trade!
Methinks he seems no bigger than his head:
The fishermen, that walk upon the beach,
Appear like mice; and yond tall anchoring bark,
Diminish'd to her cock; her cock, a buoy
Almost too small for sight: the murmuring surge,
That on the unnumber'd idle pebbles chafes,
Cannot be heard so high. I'll look no more;
Lest my brain turn, and the deficient sight
Topple down headlong.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: Set me where you stand.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l:
Give me your hand: you are now within
a foot
Of the extreme verge: for all beneath the moon
Would I not leap upright.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: Let go my hand.
Here, friend, 's another purse; in it a jewel
Well worth a poor man's taking: fairies and gods
Prosper it with thee Go thou farther off;
Bid me farewell, and let me hear thee going.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: Now fare you well, good sir.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: With all my heart.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: Why I do trifle thus with his despair
Is done to cure it.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: [Kneeling]O, you mighty gods!
This world I do renounce, and in your sights,
Shake patiently my great affliction off:
If I could bear it longer, and not fall
To quarrel with your great opposeless wills,
My snuff and loathed part of nature should
Burn itself out. If Edgar live, O, bless him!
Now, fellow, fare thee well. [He falls forward.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: Gone, sir: farewell.
And yet I know not how conceit may rob
The treasury of life, when life itself

Yields to the theft: had he been where he
thought,
By this, had thought been past. Alive or dead?
Ho, you sir! friend! Hear you, sir! speak!
Thus might he pass indeed: yet he revives.
What are you, sir?

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: Away, and let me die.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l:
Hadst thou been aught but gossamer,
feathers, air,
So many fathom down precipitating,

Thou'dst shiver'd like an egg: but thou dost
breathe;

Hast heavy substance; bleed'st not; speak'st;
art sound.
Ten masts at each make not the altitude
Which thou hast perpendicularly fell:
Thy life's a miracle. Speak yet again.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: But have I fall'n, or no?

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l:
From the dread summit of this chalky
bourn.
Look up a-height; the shrill-gorged lark so far
Cannot be seen or heard: do but look up.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: Alack, I have no eyes.
Is wretchedness deprived that benefit,
To end itself by death? 'Twas yet some comfort,
When misery could beguile the tyrant's rage,
And frustrate his proud will.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: Give me your arm:

Up: so. How is't? Feel you your legs? You
stand.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: Too well, too well.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: This is above all strangeness.
Upon the crown o' the cliff, what thing was that
Which parted from you?

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: A poor unfortunate beggar.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l:
As I stood here below, methought his
eyes
Were two full moons; he had a thousand noses,
Horns whelk'd and waved like the enridged sea:
It was some fiend; therefore, thou happy father,
Think that the clearest gods, who make them honors
Of men's impossibilities, have preserved thee.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l:
I do remember now: henceforth I'll
bear
Affliction till it do cry out itself

'Enough, enough,' and die. That thing you
speak of,
I took it for a man; often 'twould say
'The fiend, the fiend:' he led me to that place.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p:
Bear free and patient thoughts. But
who comes here?
Enter LEAR, fantastically dressed with wild
flowers. The safer sense will ne'er accommodate His master thus.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: No, they cannot touch me for coining;
I am the king himself.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: O thou side-piercing sight!

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Nature's above art in that respect. There's your press-money. That fellow handles his bow like a crow-keeper: draw me a clothier's yard. Look, look, a mouse! Peace, peace; this piece of toasted cheese will do't. There's my gauntlet; I'll prove it on a giant. Bring up the brown bills. O, well flown, bird! i' the clout, i' the clout: hewgh! Give the word.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: Sweet marjoram.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Pass.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: I know that voice.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Ha! Goneril, with a white beard! They flattered me like a dog; and told me I had white hairs in my beard ere the black ones were there. To say 'ay' and 'no' to every thing that I said!--'Ay' and 'no' too was no good divinity. When the rain came to wet me once, and the wind to make me chatter; when the thunder would not peace at my bidding; there I found 'em, there I smelt 'em out. Go to, they are not men o' their words: they told me I was every thing; 'tis a lie, I am not ague-proof.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l:
The trick of that voice I do well
remember:
Is't not the king?

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: Ay, every inch a king:
When I do stare, see how the subject quakes.
I pardon that man's life. What was thy cause?
Adultery?
Thou shalt not die: die for adultery! No:
The wren goes to't, and the small gilded fly
Does lecher in my sight.

Let copulation thrive; for Gloucester's bastard
son
Was kinder to his father than my daughters
Got 'tween the lawful sheets.
To't, luxury, pell-mell! for I lack soldiers.
Behold yond simpering dame,
Whose face between her forks presages snow;
That minces virtue, and does shake the head
To hear of pleasure's name;
The fitchew, nor the soiled horse, goes to 't
With a more riotous appetite.
Down from the waist they are Centaurs,
Though women all above:
But to the girdle do the gods inherit,
Beneath is all the fiends';

There's hell, there's darkness, there's the
sulphurous pit,
sp.p: Burning, scalding, stench, consumption; fie, fie, fie! pah, pah! Give me an ounce of civet, good apothecary, to sweeten my imagination: there's money for thee.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: O, let me kiss that hand!

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Let me wipe it first; it smells of
mortality.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l:
O ruin'd piece of nature! This great
world

Shall so wear out to nought. Dost thou know
me?

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: I remember thine eyes well enough. Dost thou squint at me? No, do thy worst, blind Cupid; I'll not love. Read thou this challenge; mark but the penning of it.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p:
Were all the letters suns, I could not
see one.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: I would not take this from report; it is,
And my heart breaks at it.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Read.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: What, with the case of eyes?

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: O, ho, are you there with me? No eyes in your head, nor no money in your purse? Your eyes are in a heavy case, your purse in a light: yet you see how this world goes.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: I see it feelingly.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: What, art mad? A man may see how this world goes with no eyes. Look with thine ears: see how yond justice rails upon yond simple thief. Hark, in thine ear: change places; and, handy-dandy, which is the justice, which is the thief? Thou hast seen a farmer's dog bark at a beggar?

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: Ay, sir.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: And the creature run from the cur? There thou mightst behold the great image of authority: a dog 's obeyed in office.
sp.l: Thou rascal beadle, hold thy bloody hand!

Why dost thou lash that whore? Strip thine own
back;
Thou hotly lust'st to use her in that kind

For which thou whipp'st her. The usurer hangs
the cozener.
Through tatter'd clothes small vices do appear;

Robes and furr'd gowns hide all. Plate sin with
gold,
And the strong lance of justice hurtless breaks;
Arm it in rags, a pigmy's straw does pierce it.

None does offend, none, I say, none; I'll able
'em:
Take that of me, my friend, who have the power
To seal the accuser's lips. Get thee glass eyes;
And, like a scurvy politician, seem

To see the things thou dost not. Now, now,
now, now:
Pull off my boots: harder, harder: so.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: O, matter and impertinency mix'd!
Reason in madness!

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l:
If thou wilt weep my fortunes, take my
eyes.
I know thee well enough; thy name is Gloucester:
Thou must be patient; we came crying hither:
Thou know'st the first time that we smell the air,
We wawl and cry. I will preach to thee: mark.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: Alack, alack the day!

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l:
When we are born, we cry that we are
come
To this great stage of fools: this' a good block;
It were a delicate stratagem, to shoe
A troop of horse with felt: I'll put't in proof;
And when I have stol'n upon these sons-in-law,

Then, kill, kill, kill, kill, kill, kill!
Enter a Gentleman, with Attendants.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l:
O, here he is: lay hand upon him.
Sir,
Your most dear daughter--

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l:
No rescue? What, a prisoner? I am
even
The natural fool of fortune. Use me well;
You shall have ransom. Let me have surgeons;
I am cut to the brains.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: You shall have any thing.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: No seconds? all myself?
Why, this would make a man a man of salt,
To use his eyes for garden water-pots,
Ay, and laying autumn's dust.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Good sir,--

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l:
I will die bravely, like a bridegroom.
What!
I will be jovial: come, come; I am a king,
My masters, know you that.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: You are a royal one, and we obey you.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p:
Then there's life in 't. Nay, if you get it, you shall get it with running. Sa, sa, sa, sa.
[Exit running; Attendants follow.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l:
A sight most pitiful in the meanest
wretch,

Past speaking of in a king! Thou hast one
daughter,
Who redeems nature from the general curse
Which twain have brought her to.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: Hail, gentle sir.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Sir, speed you: what's your will?

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l:
Do you hear aught, sir, of a battle
toward?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l:
Most sure and vulgar: every one hears
that,
Which can distinguish sound.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: But, by your favour,
How near's the other army?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l:
Near and on speedy foot; the main
descry
Stands on the hourly thought.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: I thank you, sir: that's all.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l:
Though that the queen on special cause
is here,
Her army is moved on.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l:
I thank you, sir.
[Exit Gent.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l:
You ever-gentle gods, take my breath
from me;
Let not my worser spirit tempt me again
To die before you please!

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: Well pray you, father.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: Now, good sir, what are you?

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l:
A most poor man, made tame to
fortune's blows;
Who, by the art of known and feeling sorrows,
Am pregnant to good pity. Give me your hand,
I'll lead you to some biding.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: Hearty thanks:
The bounty and the benison of heaven

To boot, and boot!
Enter OSWALD.

sp.speaker: Osw.
sp.l: A proclaim'd prize! Most happy!
That eyeless head of thine was first framed flesh
To raise my fortunes. Thou old unhappy traitor,
Briefly thyself remember: the sword is out
That must destroy thee.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: Now let thy friendly hand
Put strength enough to't. [Edgar interposes.

sp.speaker: Osw.
sp.l: Wherefore, bold peasant,
Darest thou support a publish'd traitor? Hence;
Lest that the infection of his fortune take
Like hold on thee. Let go his arm.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: Chill not let go, zir, without vurther 'casion.

sp.speaker: Osw.
sp.p: Let go, slave, or thou diest!

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: Good gentleman, go your gait, and let poor volk pass. An chud ha' bin zwaggered out of my life, 'twould not ha' bin zo long as 'tis by a vortnight. Nay, come not near th' old man; keep out, che vor ye, or ise try whether your costard or my ballow be the harder: chill be plain with you.

sp.speaker: Osw.
sp.p: Out, dunghill!

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p:
Chill pick your teeth, zir: come; no matter vor your foins.
[They fight, and Edgar knocks him down.

sp.speaker: Osw.
sp.l:
Slave, thou hast slain me: villain, take
my purse:
If ever thou wilt thrive, bury my body;
And give the letters which thou find'st about me
To Edmund earl of Gloucester; seek him out

Upon the British party: O, untimely death!
[Dies.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: I know thee well: a serviceable villain;
As duteous to the vices of thy mistress
As badness would desire.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: What, is he dead?

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: Sit you down, father; rest you

Let's see these pockets: the letters that he
speaks of
May be my friends. He's dead; I am only sorry
He had no other death's-man. Let us see:
Leave, gentle wax; and, manners, blame us not:

To know our enemies' minds, we'ld rip their
hearts;
Their papers, is more lawful. [Reads]
sp.p: 'Let our reciprocal vows be remembered. You have many opportunities to cut him off: if your will want not, time and place will be fruitfully offered. There is nothing done, if he return the conqueror: then am I the prisoner, and his bed my gaol; from the loathed warmth whereof deliver me, and supply the place for your labour. 'Your--wife, so I would say-- 'Affectionate servant, 'GONERIL.'
sp.l: O undistinguished space of woman's will!
A plot upon her virtuous husband's life;
And the exchange my brother! Here, in the sands,
Thee I'll rake up, the post unsanctified
Of murderous lechers: and in the mature time
With this ungracious paper strike the sight
Of the death-practised duke: for him 'tis well
That of thy death and business I can tell.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l:
The king is mad: how stiff is my vile
sense,
That I stand up, and have ingenious feeling
Of my huge sorrows! Better I were distract:
So should my thoughts be sever'd from my griefs,
And woes by wrong imaginations lose
The knowledge of themselves.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l:
Give me your hand:
[Drum afar off.
Far off, methinks, I hear the beaten drum:
Come, father, I'll bestow you with a friend. [Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE VII

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l:
O thou good Kent, how shall I live and
work,

To match thy goodness? My life will be too
short,
And every measure fail me.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l:
To be acknowledged, madam, is
o'er-paid.
All my reports go with the modest truth;
Nor more nor clipp'd, but so.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Be better suited:
These weeds are memories of those worser hours:
I prithee, put them off.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l: Pardon me, dear madam;
Yet to be known shortens my made intent:
My boon I make it, that you know me not
Till time and I think meet.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l:
Then be't so, my good lord. [To the
Doctor] How does the king?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Madam, sleeps still.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: O you kind gods,
Cure this great breach in his abused nature!
The untuned and jarring senses, O, wind up
Of this child-changed father!

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: So please your majesty
That we may wake the king: he hath slept long.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l:
Be govern'd by your knowledge, and
proceed
I' the sway of your own will. Is he array'd?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l:
Ay, madam; in the heaviness of his
sleep
We put fresh garments on him.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l:
Be by, good madam, when we do awake
him;
I doubt not of his temperance.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Very well.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l:
Please you, draw near. Louder the
music there!

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: O my dear father! Restoration hang
Thy medicine on my lips; and let this kiss
Repair those violent harms that my two sisters
Have in thy reverence made!

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l: Kind and dear princess!

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l:
Had you not been their father, these
white flakes
Had challenged pity of them. Was this a face
To be opposed against the warring winds?
To stand against the deep dread-bolted thunder?
In the most terrible and nimble stroke

Of quick, cross lightning? to watch--poor
perdu!--
With this thin helm? Mine enemy's dog,

Though he had bit me, should have stood that
night
Against my fire; and wast thou fain, poor father,
To hovel thee with swine, and rogues forlorn,
In short and musty straw? Alack, alack!
'Tis wonder that thy life and wits at once

Had not concluded all. He wakes; speak to
him.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: Madam, do you; 'tis fittest.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p:
How does my royal lord? How fares
your majesty?

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l:
You do me wrong to take me out o' the
grave:
Thou art a soul in bliss; but I am bound
Upon a wheel of fire, that mine own tears
Do scald like molten lead.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Sir, do you know me?

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l:
You are a spirit, I know: when did
you die?

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Still, still, far wide!

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p:
He's scarce awake: let him alone
awhile.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l:
Where have I been? Where am I?
Fair daylight?

I am mightily abused. I should e'en die with
pity,
To see another thus. I know not what to say.
I will not swear these are my hands: let's see;
I feel this pin prick. Would I were assured
Of my condition!

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: O, look upon me, sir,
And hold your hands in benediction o'er me:
No, sir, you must not kneel.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: Pray, do not mock me:
I am a very foolish fond old man,
Fourscore and upward, not an hour more nor less;
And, to deal plainly,
I fear I am not in my perfect mind.
Methinks I should know you, and know this man;
Yet I am doubtful: for I am mainly ignorant
What place this is; and all the skill I have
Remembers not these garments; nor I know not

Where I did lodge last night. Do not laugh
at me;
For, as I am a man, I think this lady
To be my child Cordelia.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: And so am I, I am.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l:
Be your tears wet? yes, 'faith. I pray,
weep not:
If you have poison for me, I will drink it.
I know you do not love me; for your sisters
Have, as I do remember, done me wrong:
You have some cause, they have not.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: No cause, no cause.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: Am I in France?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l: In your own kingdom, sir.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: Do not abuse me.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l:
Be comforted, good madam: the great
rage,
You see, is kill'd in him: and yet it is danger
To make him even o'er the time he has lost.
Desire him to go in; trouble him not more
Till further settling.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Will't please your highness walk?

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: You must bear with me:

Pray you now, forget and forgive: I am old and
foolish.
[Exeunt all but Kent and Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Holds it true, sir, that the Duke of
Cornwall was so slain?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Most certain, sir.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: Who is conductor of his people?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l: As 'tis said, the bastard son of
Gloucester.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: They say Edgar, his banished son, is with the Earl of Kent in Germany.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Report is changeable. 'Tis time to look about; the powers of the kingdom approach apace.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: The arbitrement is like to be bloody.
Fare you well, sir. [Exit.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l:
My point and period will be thoroughly
wrought,
Or well or ill, as this day's battle's fought. [Exit.

div.head: SCENE I
div.stage:
Enter, with drum and colours, EDMUND,
REGAN, Gentlemen, and Soldiers.

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.l:
Know of the duke if his last purpose
hold,
Or whether since he is advised by aught
To change the course: he's full of alteration

And self-reproving: bring his constant pleasure.
[To a Gentleman, who goes out.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: Our sister's man is certainly miscarried.

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.l: 'Tis to be doubted, madam.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: Now sweet lord,
You know the goodness I intend upon you:
Tell me--but truly--but then speak the truth,
Do you not love my sister?

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.l: In honour'd love.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l:
But have you never found my brother's
way
To the forfended place?

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.l: That thought abuses you,

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l:
I am doubtful that you have been
conjunct
And bosom'd with her, as far as we call hers.

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.p: No, by mine honour, madam.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: I never shall endure her: dear my lord,
Be not familiar with her.

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.l: Fear me not:

She and the duke her husband!
Enter, with drum and colours, ALBANY,
GONERIL, and Soldiers.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l:
[Aside]I had rather lose the battle than
that sister
Should loosen him and me.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Our very loving sister, well be-met.
Sir, this I hear; the king is come to his daughter,
With others whom the rigour of our state
Forced to cry out. Where I could not be honest,
I never yet was valiant: for this business,
It toucheth us, as France invades our land,
Not bolds the king, with others, whom I fear,
Most just and heavy causes make oppose.

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.l: Sir, you speak nobly.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: Why is this reason'd?

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: Combine together 'gainst the enemy;
For these domestic and particular broils
Are not the question here.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Let's then determine
With the ancient of war on our proceedings.

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.l: I shall attend you presently at your tent.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: Sister, you'll go with us?

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p:
'Tis most convenient; pray you, go
with us.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l:
[Aside]O, ho, I know the riddle.--I will go.
As they are going out, enter EDGAR disguised.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l:
If e'er your grace had speech with man
so poor,
Hear me one word.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l:
I'll overtake you. Speak.
[Exeunt all but Albany and Edgar.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l:
Before you fight the battle, ope this
letter.
If you have victory, let the trumpet sound
For him that brought it: wretched though I seem,
I can produce a champion that will prove
What is vouched there. If you miscarry,
Your business of the world hath so an end,
And machination ceases. Fortune love you!

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Stay till I have read the letter.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: I was forbid it.
When time shall serve, let but the herald cry,
And I'll appear again.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l:
Why, fare thee well: I will o'erlook thy
paper. [Exit Edgar.
Re-enter EDMUND.

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.l:
The enemy's in view; draw up your
powers.
Here is the guess of their true strength and forces
By diligent discovery; but your haste
Is now urged on you.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: We will greet the time. [Exit.

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.l:
To both these sisters have I sworn my
love;
Each jealous of the other, as the stung
Are of the adder. Which of them shall I take?
Both? one? or neither? Neither can be enjoy'd,
If both remain alive: to take the widow
Exasperates, makes mad her sister Goneril;
And hardly shall I carry out my side,
Her husband being alive. Now then we'll use
His countenance for the battle; which being done,
Let her who would be rid of him devise
His speedy taking off. As for the mercy
Which he intends to Lear and to Cordelia,
The battle done, and they within our power,
Shall never see his pardon; for my state
Stands on me to defend, not to debate. [Exit.

div.head: SCENE II
div.stage: A field between the two camps.

Enter, with drum and colours,
LEAR, CORDELIA, and Soldiers, over the stage;
and exeunt.
Enter EDGAR and GLOUCESTER.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l:
Here, father, take the shadow of this
tree

For your good host; pray that the right may
thrive:
If I ever I return to you again,
I'll bring you comfort.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l:
Grace go with you, sir!
[Exit Edgar.
Alarum and retreat within. Re-enter EDGAR.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l:
Away, old man; give me thy hand;
away!
King Lear hath lost, he and his daughter ta'en:
Give me thy hand; come on.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l:
No farther, sir; a man may rot even
here.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l:
What, in ill thoughts again? Men must
endure
Their going hence, even as their coming hither:
Ripeness is all: come on.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: And that's true too. [Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE III

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.l:
Some officers take them away: good
guard,
Until their greater pleasure first be known
That are to censure them.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: We are not the first
Who, with best meaning, have incurr'd the worst.
For thee, oppressed king, am I cast down;
Myself could else out-frown false fortune's frown.
Shall we not see these daughters and these sisters?

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l:
No, no, no, no! Come, let's away to
prison:
We two alone will sing like birds i' the cage:
When thou dost ask me blessing, I'll kneel down,
And ask of thee forgiveness: so we'll live,
And pray, and sing, and tell old tales, and laugh
At gilded butterflies, and hear poor rogues
Talk of court news; and we'll talk with them too,
Who loses and who wins; who's in, who's out;
And take upon's the mystery of things,
As if we were God's spies: and we'll wear out,
In a wall'd prison, packs and sects of great ones,
That ebb and flow by the moon.

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.l: Take them away.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: Upon such sacrifices, my Cordelia,

The gods themselves throw incense. Have I
caught thee?
He that parts us shall bring a brand from heaven,
And fire us hence like foxes. Wipe thine eyes;
The good-years shall devour them, flesh and fell,

Ere they shall make us weep: we'll see 'em starve
first.
Come. [Exeunt Lear and Cordelia, guarded.

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.l: Come hither, captain; hark.

Take thou this note [giving a paper]; go follow
them to prison:
One step I have advanced thee; if thou dost
As this instructs thee, thou dost make thy way
To noble fortunes: know thou this, that men
Are as the time is: to be tender-minded
Does not become a sword: thy great employment
Will not bear question; either say thou'lt do't,
Or thrive by other means.

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.l: I'll do't, my lord.

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.l:
About it; and write happy when thou
hast done.
Mark, I say, instantly; and carry it so
As I have set it down.

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.l: I cannot draw a cart, nor eat dried oats;

If it be man's work, I'll do it. [Exit.
Flourish. Enter ALBANY, GONERIL, REGAN,
another Captain, and Soldiers.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l:
Sir, you have shown to-day your valiant
strain,
And fortune led you well: you have the captives
That were the opposites of this day's strife:
We do require them of you, so to use them
As we shall find their merits and our safety
May equally determine.

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.l: Sir, I thought it fit
To send the old and miserable king
To some retention and appointed guard;
Whose age has charms in it, whose title more,
To pluck the common bosom on his side,
And turn our impress'd lances in our eyes

Which do command them. With him I sent the
queen;
My reason all the same; and they are ready
To-morrow, or at further space, to appear
Where you shall hold your session. At this time

We sweat and bleed: the friend hath lost his
friend;
And the best quarrels, in the heat are cursed
By those that feel their sharpness:
The question of Cordelia and her father
Requires a fitter place.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Sir, by your patience,
I hold you but a subject of this war,
Not as a brother.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: That's as we list to grace him.
Methinks our pleasure might have been demanded,
Ere you had spoke so far. He led our powers;
Bore the commission of my place and person;
The which immediacy may well stand up,
And call itself your brother.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: Not so hot:
In his own grace he doth exalt himself,
More than in your addition.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: In my rights,
By me invested, he compeers the best.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l:
That were the most, if he should
husband you.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: Jesters do oft prove prophets.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: Holla, holla!
That eye that told you so look'd but a-squint.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l:
Lady, I am not well; else I should
answer
From a full flowing stomach. General,
Take thou my soldiers, prisoners, patrimony;
Dispose of them, of me; the walls are thine:
Witness the world, that I create thee here
My lord and master.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: Mean you to enjoy him?

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: The let-alone lies not not in your good will.

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.l: Nor in thine, lord.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Half-blooded fellow, yes.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p:
Let the drum strike, and
prove my title thine.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l:
Stay yet; hear reason. Edmund, I
arrest thee
On capital treason; and, in thine attaint,

This gilded serpent [pointing to Gon.]. For your
claim, fair sister,
I bar it in the interest of my wife:
'Tis she is sub-contracted to this lord,
And I, her husband, contradict your bans.
If you will marry, make your loves to me,
My lady is bespoke.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: An interlude!

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l:
Thou art arm'd, Gloucester: let the
trumpet sound:
If none appear to prove upon thy head
Thy heinous, manifest, and many treasons,
There is my pledge [throwing down a glove];
I'll prove it on thy heart,
Ere I taste bread, thou art in nothing less
Than I have here proclaim'd thee.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: Sick, O, sick!

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p: If not, I'll ne'er trust medicine.

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.l:
There's my exchange [throwing down down
a glove]: what in the world he is
That names me traitor, villain-like he lies:
Call by thy trumpet: he that dares approach,
On him, on you, who not? I will maintain
My truth and honour firmly.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: A herald, ho!

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.l: A herald, ho, a herald!

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Trust to thy single virtue; for thy soldiers,
All levied in my name, have in my name
Took their discharge.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: My sickness grows upon me.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l:
She is not well; convey her to my tent.
[Exit Regan, led.
Enter a Herald.
Come hither, herald,--Let the trumpet sound,--
And read out this.

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.p: Sound, trumpet! [A trumpet sounds.

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.p: 'If any man of quality or degree within the lists of the army will maintain upon Edmund, supposed Earl of Gloucester, that he is a manifold traitor, let him appear by the third sound of the trumpet: he is bold in his defence.'

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.p: Sound! [First trumpet.

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.p: Again! [Second trumpet.

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.p:
Again! [Third trumpet. [Trumpet answers within.
Enter EDGAR, at the third sound, armed, with
a trumpet before him.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Ask him his purposes, why he appears
Upon this call o' the trumpet.

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.l: What are you?
Your name, your quality? and why you answer
This present summons?

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: Know, my name is lost;
By treason's tooth bare-gnawn and canker-bit:
Yet am I noble as the adversary
I come to cope.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Which is that adversary?

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l:
What's he that speaks for Edmund Earl
of Gloucester?

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.l: Himself: what say'st thou to him?

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.l: Draw thy sword,
